title: God is ready to do good, and slow to punish
english: God is ready to do good, and slow to punish those who deserve punishment. He could bring the penalty on those he has condemned in silence, without first bearing witness against them. He never does that. Even when he condemns, he speaks, and he speaks so that the one about to be condemned may turn from the sentence.
There are many examples of this in the Scriptures. A few that come up at once will be enough, so that we may reach the aim of the readings set before us.

The Ninevites had become sinners, and they were condemned by God. Yet three days, and Nineveh was about to be overthrown. God did not wish to condemn the city in silence. He gave them room for repentance and turning, and sent a Hebrew prophet, so that when the prophet said, 'Yet three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown,' those already condemned might not be condemned, but might repent and meet with the mercy of God.

Those in Sodom and Gomorrah had been condemned, as is clear from God's words to Abraham. Even so the angels did their part, wanting to save those who did not want to be saved. They said to Lot, 'Have you anyone here, sons-in-law or sons or daughters?' They were not ignorant that those others would not follow Lot. They were doing the work of their own kindness, and of the kindness of the one who sent them.

title: Why the dates of Jeremiah's prophecy are written
english: You will find the same thing in what is written about Jeremiah. The time of his prophecy is recorded: when he began, and how far he prophesied. Then the reader, if he does not attend to the reading and examine the intent of the passages set down, will say: this is history, and it is written when Jeremiah began to prophesy, and after how long a time he stopped. What is this history to me?

I read, and I learned that he began to prophesy 'in the days of Josiah son of Amos, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.' Then 'it came to pass in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah,' and he prophesied 'until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah son of Josiah, king of Judah.' And I learned that his prophecy stretched through three kings, 'until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month.' What then are we taught through these things, if we attend to the reading?

title: God sent the prophet before the captivity, and even in it
english: God condemned Jerusalem for her sins, and they had been judged to be left to captivity. Even so the God who loves mankind, when the time had come, sends this prophet also, starting two reigns before the captivity, so that those who were willing, taking it in, might repent through the prophetic words. He sent a prophet to prophesy under the second king after the first, and under the third, up to the very times of the captivity.

For the long-suffering God was giving a delay even, so to speak, one day before the captivity, urging those who heard to repent, so that the grim things of the captivity might cease. That is why it is written that Jeremiah prophesied 'until the captivity of Jerusalem, until the fifth month.' He had begun, and he was still prophesying, as if to say: you have become captives; even so, repent. If you repent, the captivity will not go on, but the mercy of God will stand over you.

So we have something useful from the record that gives the times of the prophecy: that God, according to his own love of mankind, urges those who hear not to suffer the things of the captivity. It is like this with us too. If we sin, we also are about to become captives. For 'to hand such a one over to Satan' differs in nothing from handing those from Jerusalem over to Nebuchadnezzar. As they were handed over to him because of sins, so we are handed over to Satan because of sins — Satan who is a Nebuchadnezzar. And 'those I handed over to Satan, that they may be taught not to blaspheme,' the apostle says of other sinners.

title: Sin hands the soul to a spiritual Babylon
english: See then how great an evil it is to sin, so that people are handed over to Satan, who takes captive the souls of those left by God. God does not leave without cause, and not without judgment, those he has left. For when he sends the rain on the vineyard, and the vineyard bears thorns instead of grapes, what will God do but 'command the clouds not to rain' on the vineyard?

Because of our sins a captivity hangs over us too, and we are about to be handed over, if we do not repent, to Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians, so that the spiritual Babylonians may tear us. With these things hanging over us, the words of the prophets, the words of the Law, the words of the apostles, the words of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, speak to us about repentance and call us to a turning. If we hear, let us believe the one who said, 'I also will repent of all the evils which I spoke of doing to them.' So much for the preface.

title: Before I formed you in the womb I knew you
english: After the preface it is written that 'the word of the Lord came to him' — clearly, to Jeremiah. And what does the word of the Lord say to him? Something set apart from what was said to the other prophets. For we have found this said to none of the prophets.

Abraham was called a prophet in the word, 'He is a prophet, and he will pray for you,' and God did not say to him, 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you.' Abraham was sanctified later, when he went out from his land and from his kindred and from his father's house. Isaac was born of promise, and we have not found this word said even to him. Why should I go through the rest? Jeremiah received a gift set apart: 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you.'

title: Some refer the words to the Savior; the whole sequence must be kept
english: We are not unaware that some refer these words, as greater than Jeremiah, to our Savior and Lord. And one must know that much of it agrees with him and can be referred to the Savior — I will set that out. But a few of the things said to Jeremiah press the argument, and cannot, as most people take them, be fitted to the Savior.

What then fits the Savior? 'To all to whom I send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their face, because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.' These would not yet clearly seem to be referred to the Savior. But what follows puts the reading about Jeremiah in a tight place: 'And the Lord stretched out his hand toward me and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me, Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down.' What nations did Jeremiah uproot? What kingdoms did he overthrow? For it is written, 'Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down.' And what authority did Jeremiah have 'to destroy'? And whom did he build in such numbers that it should be said 'and to build'? Jeremiah says, 'I have not profited, and no one has profited me.' How then is 'to build and to plant' given to him? How will 'to plant' fit Jeremiah?

These things, referred to the Savior, do not press the interpreter, because in them Jeremiah is a symbol of the Savior. But what I am about to set down presses even the most intelligent person who wants to show how these too can fit the Savior: 'And I said, You who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak.' He who is Wisdom, he who is the Power of God, who brought us 'the fullness of the deity, which dwelt in him bodily' — how then can 'I do not know how to speak' fit the Savior? And 'I am younger' is forbidden to the Savior, as if he were saying it wrongly. For if the Lord says to him, Do not say this, it is clear that he forbids what is not well said. So these do not fit the Savior. Those other words do not seem to put the Savior to shame.

To say that these belong to Jeremiah and those to the Savior is not hard. But a fair-minded person will be much pressed here. To cut a connected run of words, and to say, 'These, being lesser, fit Jeremiah and not Christ, and these, being greater than Jeremiah, fit Christ and not Jeremiah' — that is the work of people without judgment. Let the whole, then, be referred to Jeremiah, and let even the things that seem greater than Jeremiah be interpreted.

title: Nations and kingdoms in the soul; the child who chooses the good
english: Everyone who has received words from God and has the grace of the heavenly words has received them in order 'to uproot nations and kingdoms and to pull them down.' But if it is said that everyone who has received words from God 'uproots nations and kingdoms,' do not take the nations and the kingdoms for me in a bodily way. Look at human souls, ruled by sin, as the apostle said: 'Do not let sin reign in our mortal body.' And seeing the many kinds of sins, take the nations and the kingdoms as a figure: the bad things in the souls of men, which are uprooted and pulled down by the words of God given either to Jeremiah or to anyone at all.

The first things, which press us as regards the Savior, can also fit Jeremiah; and the second things can fit Jeremiah for the one who knows how to read them as a figure. Someone among the hearers will say to me: Work the other reading too, and try to show that all that is written fits the Savior. Do not be anxious about the second things. It is clear that the Savior uprooted the kingdoms of the devil and pulled down the nations, taking away the life of the nations. Here, at what seems ill-sounding as regards the Savior, work the word somehow: how can the Savior say, 'I do not know how to speak, because I am younger,' and the rest? You see that the argument is in a tight place.

We know the Savior is Lord. We are seeking, according to the dignity of the Word and according to the truth, to refer these things to the Savior. Witnesses must be taken from the Scriptures. For our guesses, if they have no witness, and our interpretations, are not to be trusted. And 'every word shall be established at the mouth of two or three witnesses' fits interpretations more than it fits men, so that I may establish the words of the interpretation by taking two witnesses from the New and the Old Covenant, taking three from gospel, from prophet, from apostle. For so every word will stand.

How then can we refer these things to the Savior? Bring the Old Covenant as a witness: 'Before the child knows good or evil, he refuses evil to choose the good.' And these things are said outright about the Savior in Isaiah: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.' And there it is added: 'before the child knows.' And if an example must also be taken from the gospel: Jesus, not yet become a man but still a child, since 'he emptied himself,' was advancing. For no one who is already perfected advances; he advances who still needs advance. So he 'advanced in stature, advanced in wisdom, advanced in grace with God and men.' If he emptied himself coming down here, and emptying himself was taking again from what he had emptied himself of, having emptied himself willingly, what is strange if he also advanced 'in wisdom and stature and grace with God and men,' and if what I set down from Isaiah is true of him: before he knows good or evil he will choose the good and refuse evil?

title: Not knowing how to speak is greater than human speech
english: But someone will say: Even if you can refer 'he does not know' to the Savior, does it not offend you to say these things about the Only-begotten, about the firstborn of all creation, about the one announced before the conception according to the word, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you'? And you say he does not know how to speak?

See whether you can see something worth saying, and great, about the Savior in this place: that not knowing certain things, he is greater in not knowing them than in knowing them. And I use his own voice as a witness that he does not know certain things. He says to those who tell him, 'Did we not eat in your name, and drink in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works?' 'Depart from me; I never knew you.' Does that 'I never knew you' present his power as lesser, or as greater and more wonderful, because he did not know the worse and those who are perishing? For he knew the things that matter, the better things, and 'the Lord knew those who are his,' and 'if anyone is ignorant, he is not known.' So the sinner is not known by God.

Someone among the hearers will say to me: You have shown that he does not know the sinners; you have shown that he does not know those who work lawlessness, for they are not worthy of his knowledge. How will you show that it is a great and glorious thing for the Savior to say, 'I do not know how to speak'? Speaking is a human thing. To speak is to use a dialect: the speech of the Hebrews, say, or of the Greeks, or of some others. If you go up to the Savior and see him as Word 'in the beginning with God,' you will see that he does not know how to speak, because speaking is human. He does not know it, because what he knows is greater than speaking. And if you compare the tongues of angels with the tongues of men, and see that he is greater even than angels, as the apostle bore witness in the letter to the Hebrews, you will say that he was greater even than the tongue of angels when he was God, the Word with the Father.

So he learns, and as it were takes on, a knowledge not of great things but of lesser and smaller ones. Just as I force myself to lisp when I talk with little children (for not knowing how to speak in baby-talk, being full-grown I force myself to talk with children), in the same way the Savior, being 'in the Father' and in the greatness of the glory of God, does not speak human things and does not know how to utter speech to those below. But when he comes into a human body he says at the beginning, 'I do not know how to speak, because I am younger.' Younger because of the bodily birth; older according to 'firstborn of all creation'; younger because he came at the completion of the ages and visited this life later. So he says, 'I do not know how to speak': I know things greater than speaking, I know things greater than this human sound. You want me to speak to men? I have not yet taken up a human dialect. I have your dialect, O God. I am your Word, O God. I know how to speak with you. I do not know how to speak to men. I am younger.

title: Formed in the womb, not made: God knows those who are his
english: Whether it is said to Jeremiah or to the Savior, 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you': if you read Genesis and watch what is said about the making of the world, you will find that the Scripture, with a very fine distinction, did not say, 'Before I made you in the womb I know you.' For when the one according to the image was being created, 'God said, Let us make man according to our image and likeness.' He did not say, Let us form. But when he took 'dust from the earth,' he did not make the man; he 'formed the man,' and 'placed in the garden the man whom he had formed, to work it and to keep it.'

If you can, see the difference between making and forming. The Lord, whether to Jeremiah or to the Savior, did not say, 'Before I made you in the womb I know you.' For what is made does not come about in the womb; what is formed from the dust of the earth is created in the womb. 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you.' If the Lord knew all, he would not have said to Jeremiah as something set apart, 'I know you.' So God knows those who matter, God knows those worthy of his knowledge, and 'the Lord knew those who are his.' Those unworthy God does not know, as the Savior also does not: 'I never knew you.'

We, being men, as we advance, judge some things worthy of our knowing them. Some things we do not even want to hear, so that we may not know them. Some things we want to know. What of the God of all? Does he want to know Pharaoh? Does he want to know the Egyptians? They are not worthy of the knowledge of God. Moses is worthy, and each of the prophets of that rank. You must set many things right before God begins to know you. Jeremiah he knew before forming him in the womb. Another he begins to know at thirty years of age, another at forty. There are secret words here, not in question as regards the Savior, but as regards Jeremiah needing attention from those who have ears.

title: A prophet to the nations
english: 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations.' If it is a matter of the higher sense: if of Jeremiah, we have already spoken; if of the Savior, what need is there even to say it? He truly prophesied to all the nations. For he is, as he is ten thousand other things, also a prophet. As he is high priest, as he is savior, as he is physician, so he is also prophet. Moses, prophesying about him, did not say only 'a prophet,' but said it with a special force: 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your brothers, like me; him you shall hear, and it shall be that whoever does not hear that prophet shall be destroyed from his people.'

This one, then, is also the prophet set 'to the nations,' and he received grace from God poured out on his lips, so that not only when he was present in the body, but also now, when he is present in power and in the Spirit, he may prophesy 'to all the nations,' so that from all the nations his prophecy may reach its end and draw men to salvation.

title: A child in body, a grown man within; do not fear their face
english: 'And I said, You who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am younger. And the Lord said to me, Do not say that I am younger, because to all to whom I send you...' We have often said that it is possible, according to the inner man, to be a child, even if someone is in an old age of body. And it is possible at times, according to the outer man, to be a child, and according to the inner, a man. Such was Jeremiah, already having the grace from God while he was still in the age of a child according to the body. That is why the Lord says to him, 'Do not say that I am younger.' And a sign that he is not younger, but 'a grown man,' is this: 'To all to whom I send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their face.'

The Word of God knows that those who serve as ambassadors of the word are in danger among the hearers. For when they are exposed they hate them; when they are rebuked they persecute them. The prophets suffer every kind of thing. 'A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his house' — which we also recalled earlier. So God, sending the prophet, knows how many dangers he will take on, and he says to him, 'Do not be afraid of their face, because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.'

What Jeremiah suffered is written down. He was thrown into a pit of mire; he remained there eating one loaf a day and drinking water only; and ten thousand other things which his prophecy has made clear. 'Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?' it is said to the Jews. And it is necessary that 'those who want to live in a godly way in Christ Jesus be persecuted in every case by opposing powers, through the vessels they find.' Therefore those who are persecuted must not be surprised, but must do everything, only praying that they be persecuted unjustly and not justly — not for injustice, not for sin, not for greed. And if someone is ever persecuted for righteousness, let him also hear, 'Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every evil word against you, lying, for my sake. Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is great in the heavens; for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.'

title: The Lord's own hand, not Isaiah's coal; kingdoms of the vices
english: 'Because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord. And the Lord stretched out his hand toward me, and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me.' Watch the difference between Jeremiah and Isaiah. Isaiah says, 'I have unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.' And since he confessed that he did not have unclean works, but only small words (for to that point he was a sinner), the Lord did not stretch out his hand. One of the seraphim touched his lips with his hand, and said, 'Behold, I have taken away your iniquities.' But because this one was sanctified 'from the womb,' no tongs are sent to him, and no coal 'from the altar' (he had nothing worthy of the fire). The Lord's own hand touched him. That is why he says, 'The Lord stretched out his hand toward me and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me, Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot.'

Who is so blessed as to uproot, by the words given by God, the many kingdoms which 'the devil shows,' kingdoms of opposing powers, kingdoms according to the sins? For it is written, 'Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot.' And as there are kingdoms, so there are nations. A kingdom cannot even be called a kingdom unless it has nations under it. For example: there is a kingdom of fornication, and the nations of fornication are each several fornication. There is one kingdom, the general sin of greed and of robbery, and there are many kingdoms in those who have many kinds of sins. Then, in each of the sinners, think of the nations under the kingdom: this man has many nations of the kingdom according to fornication, that man has many nations of the kingdom according to robbery, according to slander, according to anger.

It is the work of the words of God, sent out over 'nations and kingdoms,' 'to uproot and to pull down.' To uproot what? The Savior taught, saying, 'Every plant which my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.' There are some things inside in the souls which 'the heavenly Father did not plant.' For all 'the evil reasonings, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witnesses, blasphemies' are plants planted not by the heavenly Father. And if you want to see whose plants such reasonings are, hear that 'an enemy man did this,' the one who sowed 'the tares in the midst of the wheat.' So God stands by, having the seeds, and the devil. If we give 'place to the devil,' 'the enemy' sows a plant 'which the Father did not plant,' which will certainly be uprooted. If we do not give 'place to the devil,' but give place to God, God rejoices and sows his seeds on our governing mind.

Do not think, then, that Jeremiah received some grim gift from God, because he is set 'over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot.' God is good, uprooting through the words the bad things, the kingdoms hostile to the kingdom of the heavens, the warring nations against the nation of God. 'To uproot and to pull down.'

title: What is pulled down must also be destroyed
english: There is a building of the devil, and there is a building of God. The building 'on the sand' is the devil's, for it stands on nothing firm and sure and united. The building 'on the rock' is God's. See what is said to those of God: 'You are God's field, God's building.' So the words of God are over 'nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' If something is uprooted, and what was uprooted is not destroyed, it is still there. If something is pulled down, and the stones of the demolition are not destroyed, it is still there.

It is a work of the goodness of God, after the uprooting, to destroy what has been uprooted, and after the taking-down, to destroy what has been taken down. Read carefully how such things are destroyed: 'Burn the chaff with unquenchable fire,' and 'Bind the tares in bundles and hand them over to fire.' So after being uprooted they are destroyed. And if you want to see also the things destroyed after demolition, of the building of poor stuff: that house which was taken down because of leprosy becomes dust, and being dust it is thrown 'outside the city,' so that not even a stone remains, like 'I will grind them as the mud of the streets.' For the worse things must in no way still stand. Something has been pulled down: let the stones not be useful for another building which the evil one can build. Something has been uprooted: let him not again find seeds from the uprooted things, so as to sow the tares once more. For having the seeds of the tares he certainly sowed them. That is why 'bind the tares and burn them with fire,' so that after being uprooted they may be destroyed, and after being pulled down the devil's building may be destroyed.

title: Then build and plant; I will kill and I will make alive
english: But the words of God do not stop at 'to uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' Suppose the bad things have been uprooted from me, the worse things pulled down: what good is it to me if, in place of what was uprooted, the better things are not planted? What good is it to me if, in place of these, the things that matter are not built up? That is why the words of God first, of necessity, do the 'uproot and pull down and destroy,' and after that the 'build and plant.' And we have always watched in Scripture that the things which look grim, if I may call them so, are named first, then the things that seem cheerful are said second. 'I will kill and I will make alive.' He did not say, 'I will make alive,' and after that, 'I will kill.' For it is impossible that what God has made alive should be taken away by him or by anyone else. But 'I will kill and I will make alive.' Whom will I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor. 'And I will make alive,' so that he may become 'Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ.'

If the wretched people from the heresies had understood these things, they would not keep putting them forward to us, saying, Do you see how fierce and inhuman the God of the Law is, when he says, 'I will kill, and I will make alive'? Do you not see in the Scriptures a promise of the resurrection of the dead? Or do you not see the resurrection of the dead already making its beginning in each person? 'We were buried' with Christ 'through baptism' and we were raised with him.

So he begins from the grimmer voices, which are necessary — as 'I will kill' — then, having killed, 'and I will make alive. I will strike, and I will heal.' 'For whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives.' First he strikes, and after that he heals. 'For he makes one feel pain and again restores.' So also here: 'I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down and to destroy and to build and to plant.' Only, first those bad things must be taken from us. God cannot build on the place of the bad building. 'For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness?' Vice must be uprooted from the foundations. The building of vice must be consumed from our soul, so that after these things the words of God may build and plant.

I cannot understand what is written in any other way: 'Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.' What do the words do? 'To uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' Words uproot 'nations'; words pull down kingdoms — not these worldly ones. Think, in a way worthy of words that pull down, worthy of words that uproot, the things uprooted by words, the things pulled down by words. Is there not, in what is being said right now, a power — if God gives it (according to 'the Lord will give a word to those who preach good news with great power') — a power that uproots, if there is any unbelief, any hypocrisy, any vice, any incontinence? Is there not a power that pulls down, if somewhere an idol-shrine has been built in the heart, so that when that is pulled down a temple of God may be built, and the glory of God may be found in the temple built up, and there may be not a grove but a planting, a garden of God, where the temple of God is, in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power to the ages of the ages. Amen.

title: God did not make death; how did the true vine turn bitter
english: 'God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living. For he created all things that they might be, and the generations of the world are saving, and there is no poison of ruin in them, nor a kingdom of Hades upon the earth.' Then, going a little past the wording, I will say from where death entered: 'By the envy of the devil death entered into the world.' So whatever is best about us, God has made; but we have created evil and sins for ourselves.

That is why here too the beginning of the reading in the prophet was speaking, as it were questioningly, to those who have had bitterness in the soul, opposite to the sweetness which God prepared for it: 'How have you turned into bitterness, the alien vine?' As if he were saying: God did not make lameness, but he made all sound of foot — what then has become the cause of those who have been lamed? And God made all the members healthy in the first place — what has become a cause of someone suffering something?

In the same way the soul has come to be 'according to the image' not of the first man only, but of every man. For 'let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness' reaches to all men. And as in Adam that which most people understand as 'according to the image' is older than what was added to him when, because of sin, he wore 'the image of the dusty one,' so in all the 'according to the image of God' is older than the worse image. 'We have worn,' being sinners, 'the image of the dusty one; let us wear,' repenting, 'the image of the heavenly one.' Yet the creation came to be in the image of the heavenly one.

So here the Word is at a loss toward those who sin, speaking as a reproof: 'How have you turned into bitterness, the alien vine? For I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, all true.' In what was said before this it has been spoken, and taking up a little I will persuade you that God planted a good vine, the soul of man, and each, having turned, has become opposite to the will of the one who created him. 'And I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, all' — not in part — 'true,' not one true and one false, but 'I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, all true. How have you turned' — I planted you an all-true vine; you, how have you turned into bitterness and become an alien vine?

title: Nitre and soap cannot wash every stain
english: After this let us look at: 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained in your injustices before me, says the Lord.' Did some sinning soul suppose that, taking nitre and washing with ordinary nitre, it ceases from the stain and ceases from the sin? Did someone assume that, taking this herb that springs from the earth and washing and scouring, the soul is cleansed, because the Word says here to the one who has turned into bitterness and become an alien vine, 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained in your injustices before me, says the Lord'?

But one must know that the Word has all power. And as he has the power of all Scripture, so the Word has the power of every medicine, and is the power of everything that cleanses, and is most scouring. 'For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword.' And whatever you name, of which there is need, that is in the power of the Word. So there is a word that is nitre, and there is a word that is soap, which, when spoken, cleanses such filth. But since not every sin is healed from such a word as is nitre, and from such a word as is soap — there are sins that do not need nitre or soap — it is said to the one who thinks it has sins of a kind that can be washed off in nitre and soap: 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained before me in your injustices, says the Lord.'

And as of wounds some are healed with a poultice, and others with oil, and others need a bandage and so are made well, and there are other wounds of which it is said, 'There is no poultice to put on, nor oil nor bandages; but your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire' — so there are some sins which soil the soul, and for these sins the man needs a word that is nitre, a word that is soap. And there are some sins which are not healed this way, for they are not even compared to soil. That is why the Lord in Isaiah, knowing the differences of sins, see how he says, 'The Lord will wash the soil of the sons and of the daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst with a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.' Soil and blood: soil with a spirit of judgment, blood with a spirit of burning. If you have sinned, yet not 'unto death,' you have been soiled. So 'the Lord will wash the soil of the sons and of the daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst.' Then the matching: toward 'the soil,' 'with a spirit of judgment'; toward 'the blood,' 'with a spirit of burning.' And most of us, if we have sinned the worse things, do not need nitre, nor the multiplying of soap, but the spirit of burning.

title: Baptism in the Holy Spirit, and baptism in fire
english: That is why Jesus baptizes (perhaps I find the meaning now) 'in the Holy Spirit and fire.' Not that he baptizes the same person 'in the Holy Spirit and fire,' but the holy one 'in the Holy Spirit,' and the one who, after believing, after being counted worthy of the Holy Spirit, has sinned again, he washes in 'fire' — so that it is not the same person being baptized by Jesus 'in the Holy Spirit and fire.' Blessed, then, is the one baptized in the Holy Spirit and not needing the baptism from fire. Thrice-wretched is that one who has need to be baptized with the fire. Yet Jesus has both. 'For a rod will come out of the root of Jesse, and a flower will go up from the root.' A 'rod' upon those being punished; a 'flower' upon the righteous. So 'God is a consuming fire,' and 'God is light': a consuming fire to sinners, light to the righteous and holy.

And blessed is the one who has a part in the first resurrection, who has kept the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Who is the one saved in another resurrection? The one who needs the baptism from fire, when he comes to that fire, and the fire tests him, and that fire finds wood, hay, and stubble, so as to burn them. Therefore, these things being said, gathering as far as we can the words of the Scriptures, let us store them in the heart and try to live according to them, if perhaps we may be able to become clean before the departure, and, having prepared our works for the departure, going out may be taken up in those good things and be saved in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power to the ages of the ages. Amen.

title: First to Israel, then to the nations
english: Acts says it plainly: the apostles went first into the synagogues of the Jews. They announced to them, as kin through Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, what Scripture had written about the coming of Jesus Christ.

When those hearers would not receive what was said, others had to hear it. So the apostles made their defense and left them. Scripture records: 'It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first. Since you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, look—we turn to the Gentiles.'

What Acts states with force in many places the prophets also said. The Holy Spirit speaks first through the holy prophets to that people. But when much has been spoken and not heard, the Spirit prophesies the word that will be preached to the nations.

The same turn happens at the start of today's reading. Before this, Israel heard: 'Even if you call me Father and do not turn away from me, yet as a woman deals treacherously with her companion, so the house of Israel has dealt treacherously with me,' says the Lord. And they heard that they had done wrong in their ways and forgotten their holy God. Then the Holy Spirit shifts the word to us who come from the nations and says: 'Return, you turning children, and I will heal your broken places.'

We are the ones filled with broken places. Each of us could say, even if now cleansed and healed: 'We too were once foolish, led astray, enslaved to many and varied desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hated and hating one another. But when the kindness and love of God our Savior appeared, he poured out his mercy on us through the washing of rebirth.'

Paul, an apostle from Israel—blameless according to the righteousness in the law—does not say only that the nations were once foolish. He says, 'We also were once disobedient and foolish.' Not only those from the nations were foolish, not only they were disobedient and sinful. We who were taught the law were the same before Christ's coming. So after the words addressed to Israel, the word turns to us from the nations: 'Return, you turning children, and I will heal your broken places.'

title: We from the nations answer, “We will be yours”
english: Someone will object: 'Those words were spoken to Israel, yet you drag them over to people from the nations.' We want to show that whenever God means to speak to Israel about turning back, he does not wait long—he adds Israel's name at once.

Next it says: 'If Israel returns to me, says the Lord, he will return; if he removes his abominations from his mouth and stands in awe before my face and swears, “As the Lord lives,” in truth, judgment, and righteousness, then nations will bless themselves in him.' So the earlier words were spoken to those from the nations. For when the fullness of the nations enters, then all Israel will be saved, as the apostle writes to the Romans.

See how God urges us who are turning to turn completely. He promises that if we turn to him as people who turn, he will heal our broken places through Jesus Christ. We answer—not delaying over salvation as that Israel did—'Here we are; we will be yours.'

God said, 'Return, you turning children, and I will heal your broken places.' Those from the nations reply that we will be his servants. We were not his before; we belonged to demons and opposing powers. When the Most High divided the nations, we did not become his portion or Jacob's inheritance allotment; we became portions of others. Yet when he said to us, 'Return, you turning children, and I will heal your broken places,' we who once were other portions answer, 'Here we are.' This is the call we were waiting for. They were called and refused; we who are called do not refuse in the same way.

In the Gospel parables some of those first invited said, 'I have married a wife; excuse me,' and another, 'I have bought five yoke of oxen and am going to test them; excuse me.' We from the nations are not called and then refuse like that. Over what field would we settle? Over what wise wife? Over what else would we busy ourselves? God has said to us, 'Return, you turning children, and I will heal your broken places.' Seeing our broken places and the promise of healing, we answer at once: 'Look—we will be yours, for you are the Lord our God.'

Having heard and said, 'We will be yours,' let us remember that we promised God that very thing. Having said it, let us become nothing else—not a spirit of anger, not a spirit of grief, not a spirit of desire, not the devil, not his angels. Called, and having said, 'Look—we will be yours,' let us show to those left desolate that we have dedicated ourselves to him alone. We say, 'For you are the Lord our God.' We confess no other god—not the belly, as gluttons do, 'whose god is the belly'; not silver, as the greedy do, nor greed, which is idolatry; nor anything else that many deify. For us the God over all is God—over all, through all, and in all. Because love binds us to God, we say: 'Here we are; we will be yours, for you are the Lord our God.'

title: False hills and the power of the mountains
english: Then, having condemned our former evils—when we thought the idols great and high, worshiped them, and counted marvelous what we served, though now we know all that was false and amounted to nothing—we say as we turn back: 'Truly the hills were for a lie.' We have condemned those former heights and marvels. And perhaps, if we work the craft carefully, we will find the difference between the hills and mountains among the nations. Those who said, 'Look—here we are; we will be yours, for you are the Lord our God,' left them and accuse both hills and mountains as false.

What, then, is the difference among the nations between mountains and hills, which we condemn when we say, 'Truly the hills were for a lie, and the power of the mountains'? Among the nations some things are worshiped as gods, others as heroes.

They themselves admit about certain ones that they were men first and were deified. They worship Heracles not as a god by birth, but as a man changed into a god. They worship Asclepius as changed from men into a god through virtue. But when they worship the fathers of these, whom they name gods, they worship them not as changed from men into gods, but—as they suppose—as gods from the beginning. So those thought gods from the beginning are the mountains and 'the power of the mountains,' while those now thought gods who were once men are 'the hills.'

Knowing both kinds of worshiped ranks, we say: 'Truly the hills were for a lie, and the power of the mountains.' Those who serve them do not suppose these things false. So they think the oracles and the healings true healings. They do not see the difference between every power and sign and wonder of falsehood in every deceit of injustice among those who are perishing—so that the fullness of the nations might enter, and after that all Israel be saved. Christ Jesus, to whom be the glory and the power forever and ever. Amen.
Therefore, recognizing these things, we who have recognized them say: 'Truly the hills were for a lie, and the power of the mountains.'

title: Remnant of Israel after the nations’ fullness
english: Then, since we who come from the nations know that by Israel's trespass we received a way of salvation, and that they are cast outside until our fullness enters—and since we know that when the fullness of the nations enters, after that all Israel will be saved—we say first, 'Truly the hills were for a lie, and the power of the mountains,' and second, concerning Israel after the fullness of the nations: 'Yet through the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel.'

Having recalled the apostolic saying—that by the trespass in which Israel fell, salvation came to the nations, and that when the fullness of the nations enters, while Israel remains outside, then after that entering fullness all Israel will be saved—let us unfold what belongs to these places. Israel was being saved.

The greater part of Israel fell, yet 'a remnant according to the election of grace has come to be,' about which remnant it is said mystically in Elijah: 'I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.' Interpreting that remnant, the apostle says: 'So then, at the present time also a remnant according to the election of grace has come to be.' So Israel is saved even as a remnant, while Israel has been left.

If you can, transfer these two ranks also onto those from the nations. He did not say, 'When all the nations are saved, then all Israel will be saved,' but, 'When the fullness of the nations enters'—then not that some Israelite is saved after all the nations, but after 'the fullness of the nations.'

If anyone can, let him take the rest as he found Israel being saved after the fullness of the nations, and by moving through the word consider when all will serve—according to what was said—'God under one yoke,' and 'sacrifices from the ends of Ethiopia'; when, as the sixty-seventh Psalm says, 'Ethiopia will stretch out her hand to God,' and the word commands the kingdoms of the earth: 'Sing to the Lord; make music to the God of Jacob.'
translator_notes: πλήρωμα τῶν Μνῶν in the lock read as ἐθνῶν with Romans 11.

title: Shame that consumes the fathers’ toil
english: So we who come from the nations say about ourselves, repenting of the false things we once counted true: 'Truly the hills and the power of the mountains were for a lie.' And about Israel who will be saved after us: 'Yet through the Lord our God is the salvation of the house of Israel.' Whether we are confessing the sins in which our fathers stood and in which we ourselves were idolaters, we say: 'Shame has consumed the labors of our fathers from their youth—their sheep and their cattle, their sons and their daughters.' Shame has consumed the labors of our fathers—and what follows.

If the wicked toil and false work of the fathers is to be consumed, shame must come first. Before shame, the fathers' toil is not consumed, nor what is added to it. So let us notice differences among those who sin. Some sin and feel no shame, no reverence over their sins, no blush. Such are those who have grown callous and handed themselves over to every licentiousness and every impurity. For people from the nations sometimes list their fornications and adulteries as if they were feats of valor. They are not even ashamed to confess they have done such things, and they do not call them sins.

As long as they are not ashamed, their toils are not consumed. Their sins are not consumed. The beginning of good things is to be ashamed of what one was not ashamed of. That is why I do not take as a curse what the prophets say: 'Let all who hate Zion be ashamed and confounded.' The prayer is that those numb to shameful works come to awareness, so that once ashamed they can consume their toils and their sins.

title: The good shepherd within rules irrational motions
english: The irrational motions of the fathers he called 'sheep' and 'calves.' Not every irrational thing is praiseworthy. Some are blameworthy, like the sheep of fathers who have sinned. Some irrational things are praiseworthy, as when he says, 'My sheep hear my voice.' Those too were sheep, and we have something analogous in the word. We have the good shepherd in our souls.

When the Savior says, 'I am the good shepherd,' I do not hear only what everyone hears—that he is shepherd of those who believe (that is sound and true). I must also have Christ within my soul, the good shepherd within me, shepherding the irrational motions in me so they no longer go out to pasture at random, but, led by the shepherd, what was once alien to him becomes his own.
Therefore now, if the shepherd is in me, he rules my senses. They are no longer under an alien mind, or under Pharaoh, or under Nebuchadnezzar, but under the good shepherd.

title: Shame consumes the fathers’ toil—or good tillage offers firstlings
english: 'Shame,' then, 'has consumed the labors of our fathers from their youth—their sheep and their oxen.' What is there in us that is tilling us—whether tilling badly (so that 'badly' is said of the tiller) or tilling well? If it tills badly, that is labor of the fathers being consumed by their shame. If it tills well, it is not the fathers' labor, but labor from which the firstborn are offered upon God's altar. They say 'their sons and their daughters.' Whose 'their'? Are the sons of 'them' or of 'the fathers' consumed by their shame? And we have often said that the offspring of the soul are these: thoughts are sons, and the works and bodily practices are daughters.

Since there are wicked thoughts—such as those from the nations thought—and wicked works as well, sons and daughters are consumed by those who made them, if shame arises in them over what was sinned. May it not be that we make sons and daughters for a consumption that comes from shame.
translator_notes: γεωρηοῦν / γεωργοῦν: OCR damage; read as γεωργοῦν ('tilling').

title: Dishonor as the veil over the heart
english: After this, those who confess say, 'We slept in our shame,' and then, 'Our dishonor covered us.' Much has been said to us about the veil that lies on the face of those who do not turn to the Lord. Because of that veil, when Moses is read, the sinner does not understand him; a veil lies on his heart. Because of that veil, when the old covenant is read, the hearer does not understand. Because of that veil the gospel also is veiled to those who are perishing. So we were saying about the veil that shame is the veil.

As long as we have 'the works of shame,' it is clear that we have the veil, according to what is said somewhere in the forty-third Psalm: 'And the shame of my face covered me.' I have set beside this that the one who has no works of shame has no veil—as Paul was, saying, 'We all, with unveiled face, behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord.' Paul has an unveiled face; he does not have works of shame. The one who is not like Paul has a veiled face.

As there it is said in the forty-third Psalm, 'The shame of my face covered me,' so here: 'Our dishonor covered us.' As long as we do works of dishonor, we have a veil lying on our heart. If we want to put away the veil that comes from dishonor, let us arrive at works of honor and understand what the Savior said: 'That all may honor the Son as they honor the Father,' and what the apostle said: 'Through the transgression of the law you dishonor God.' The righteous honors the Son as he honors the Father.

Dishonor—when I dishonor the Son (the same dishonor by which I dishonor the Father or the Son)—becomes a covering over my face, and I say, 'Our dishonor covered us.' So, understanding the veil that lies from works of shame and from such practices, let us take the veil away. It is in our power for the veil to be removed; it belongs to no one else. For when Moses turned to the Lord, the veil was taken away.

Do you see how Moses is sometimes taken also for the people? As long as he did not turn to the Lord, being a symbol of the people that does not turn to the Lord, he had a veil lying on his face. But when he turned to the Lord, becoming a symbol of those who turn to the Lord, then 'the veil was taken away.' It was not as if God commanded him, 'Put on the veil'—for the Lord did not say to Moses, 'Put the veil on'—but Moses, seeing that the people could not look at his glory, then put 'the veil on his face,' and he did not wait for God to say, 'Take away the veil,' whenever he turned to the Lord.
translator_notes: Psalm numbering follows the locked Greek (τεσσαρακοστῷ καὶ τρίτῳ).

title: Turn to the Lord and take away the veil
english: This was written so that you too—having put the veil on your face through works of dishonor and shame—may yourself also work the taking away of the veil. If you turn to the Lord, then you take away the veil, and you will no longer say, 'Our dishonor covered us.' Anger lying on our soul against someone, for example, is a veil lying on our face. Therefore if we want to pray, 'The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord,' let us take away the veil and do what the apostle teaches.

As long as these things are in our mind and reasoning, the veil and the dishonor lie on the inward face—on our ruling principle—so that we do not see the glory of God shining. It is not God who hides his glory from us; we ourselves put the veil from wickedness on the ruling principle.

title: “We have sinned,” not “we are sinning”
english: 'For we have sinned against our God, we and our fathers.' Would that we also would say it as these do, according to the prophet's personification.

'We have sinned.' 'We have sinned' is not the same as 'we are sinning.' The one still in sin should not say 'we have sinned'; the one who sinned before and has carefully repented should say 'we have sinned'—as also in Daniel there is written the confession of those no longer sinning: 'We have sinned, we have acted lawlessly,' and in the Psalms: 'Do not remember our ancient lawless deeds,' the prophet says. So let us also confess our sins—would that they were not yesterday's, would that they were not three days old, but would that in confessing we confess sins done fifteen years ago, by having no sin after those for fifteen years. But if we sinned yesterday, we are not yet trustworthy when we confess our sins; nor is there yet room for these sins of ours to be wiped away. 'For we have sinned, we and our fathers, from our youth until this day.'

Let that stand otherwise as teaching about the best manner of confession. These words are an accusation of long sinning. 'From youth,' it says, 'until this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the Lord our God.' We have sinned, and we have not obeyed until the present. Then, turning and having a beginning of turning, they say, 'We have sinned, and we have not obeyed.' For not at the same moment of wanting to obey do we already obey at once. Time is still needed, as with wounds toward healing, so also with turning—toward turning completely and purely to God.

title: Complete turning and abominations of the mouth
english: Upon these things God says concerning Israel: 'If Israel turns to me, says the Lord, he will also turn'—that is, if he turns completely, he will turn with a turning, not if he merely begins, as it were, to turn. Then he says: 'And if he removes his abominations from his mouth, and stands in awe before my face, and swears, “As the Lord lives,” in truth and in judgment and in righteousness, then nations will bless themselves in him.'

If they do these things, 'nations will bless themselves in him.' What must they do so that nations bless themselves in him? 'If he removes his abominations from his mouth.' What is removing abominations from the mouth? Whatever we speak badly are abominations in our mouth. So let us remove the abominations from our mouth, taking away slanders, empty words, idle words that will make us answerable on the day of judgment—'for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.'

Next is also, 'You will stand in awe before my face.' Let us do this second thing, not simply so that we may be reverent. For there can be a reverence that does not come from the face of God. Those who fear without knowledge, though they propose to fear, do not stand in awe from the face of God. But as many as stand in awe with knowledge—by always looking and painting for themselves the face of God that comes upon those who do evil, to wipe out their memory from the earth—these are the ones who stand in awe from the face of God.

title: Swear in truth, judgment, and righteousness
english: 'If he removes his abominations from his mouth, and stands in awe before my face, and swears: “As the Lord lives,” in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.'

Let us look at ourselves who swear—how we do not swear in judgment but without judgment, so that our oaths come by habit rather than by judgment. We are carried away, and the word, exposing this, says: 'And if he swears, “As the Lord lives,” in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.' We know what the Lord said to the disciples in the Gospel: 'But I say to you, do not swear at all.' Let us look at this saying too; and if God grants, both will be examined together. Perhaps one must first swear 'in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.'

In the one who swears I first look for what is not false but true, so that he may swear with truth. Yet we wretched ones even swear falsely. But even if it is 'with truth,' an oath is still not well made unless it is also 'in judgment.' For grant that I swear by habit—I do not swear 'in judgment.' If one must take for such an oath the God of all and his Christ upon this matter, how great must the matter be before I bend the knee and swear? Perhaps I would do it sometime to heal unbelief that has arisen in some about my word.
He has joined both—those from the nations and Israel. He spoke about the nations; he spoke also about Israel.

title: Break new ground; do not sow among thorns
english: He adds: 'And nations will bless themselves in him, and in him they will praise God in Jerusalem. For thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem.' He has spoken to those from the nations, and he has spoken to those from Israel; he speaks to those from Judah. I remember the figurative readings said earlier about Judah and those dwelling in Jerusalem. For we dwell—if God grants—in Jerusalem.

Since 'where the treasure is, there the heart is also,' if we store up treasure in heaven, we also have the heart in the Jerusalem above, about which the apostle says: 'But the Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother,' as it is written, and what follows. So 'thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem: Break new ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.' This word is spoken especially to those who teach, so that they not entrust what is said to the hearers before they make new ground in their souls. For when, putting hand to the plow, they make new ground in souls—according to the good and fine soil of those who hear—then as they sow they do not sow among thorns.

But if, before the plow and before making new ground in the ruling principle of the hearers, someone takes the holy seeds—the word about the Father, about the Son, about the Holy Spirit, about resurrection, about punishment, about rest, about law, about prophets, and in short about each of the things written—and sows them, he transgresses the command that says first, 'Break new ground for yourselves,' and second, 'Do not sow among thorns.'

But one of the hearers will say: 'I do not teach; I am not under this command.' You too become a farmer of yourself, and do not sow among thorns, but make new ground for me in the plot God of all has entrusted to you. Consider the plot; see where the thorns are—where cares of life and deceit of wealth and love of pleasure are. Having seen the thorns in your soul, seek the rational plow about which Jesus says, 'No one who puts hand to the plow and turns back is fit for the kingdom of God.' Having sought it and found it, gathering from the Scriptures the pure working oxen, plow and renew the land, and so that it may no longer be old, make it new—putting off the old man with his practices and putting on the new man renewed into knowledge. You will make new ground for yourself, and if you make the new ground, take seeds from those who teach, take seeds from the law, from the prophets, from the Gospel writings, from the apostolic words, and having taken these seeds sow the soul through memory and study. They will seem to spring up of themselves; but in truth after the memory of them it is not they that spring up, but God who grows them: 'I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.' And if anyone has been able to understand the Scriptures, that one has made new ground, and having made it has sown not among thorns. These seeds are managed by God not to become an ear all at once, but as in the Gospel according to Mark: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain.

When it is ready for harvest, those sent out upon the harvest will come. When it is ready for harvest, they will come to whom the word says: 'Lift up your eyes and see the fields, that they are already white for harvest.' So he says to us: 'Break new ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.' But if, before you cleanse your soul, while you still have thorns, you approach one who can teach or is thought to teach, or ask for lessons and spiritual seeds, you transgress the command that says, 'Do not sow among thorns.'

title: Circumcise to your God the foreskin of the heart
english: And next to this it is said: 'Be circumcised to your God; circumcise the foreskin of your heart.' 'Be circumcised to your God'—necessarily is added 'to your God.' You will understand it from the sensible example. According to the sensible I say: not only those of the circumcision according to Moses' law are circumcised, but many others also. The priests of the Egyptians' idols are circumcised, but that circumcision is circumcision to idols and is not circumcision done to God. The Jews' circumcision, perhaps—and certainly then—was done to God.

So when the word says, 'Be circumcised to your God,' understand the saying and move also to the figurative reading, so that you find how, among figurative circumcisions (so that some of them might even say, 'We are the circumcision'), some are circumcised to God, and others are circumcised, yet not to God. There are also other words besides the word of truth, besides the word of the church. Those who philosophize chastise manners and the heart, and those from the heresies chastise, and circumcision happens for them. But it is circumcision, yet not to God; for circumcision happens among them by a false word.

But when according to the church's rule, according to the aim of sound teaching, you are in communion, you are not only circumcised—you are circumcised 'to God.' So 'Be circumcised to your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart.' Who does not pass these words by as clear? So there is a foreskin of the heart, and this must be circumcised.

The one who works the word carefully, searching such things in this place, will examine: foreskin is born with us; circumcision is acquired; and what has come from birth, circumcision removes. If then the word commands the foreskin of the heart to be removed, there must be something born with the heart which he calls foreskin, which must be removed so that someone may be circumcised as to the foreskin of the heart. If anyone understands, 'We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest'; if anyone understands 'the body of our humiliation' in which we were born; if anyone understands, 'No one is clean from filth, not even if his life is one day; his months are numbered'—he will see how we were born with uncleanness and with the foreskin of our heart.

title: False opinions as the foreskin the word cuts away
english: So that it may be said according to a simpler example able to lead you to see 'the foreskin of the heart,' I will set beside this that in the first age false opinions certainly arise in the soul. For it is not possible for a human being from the beginning to take true doctrines. The divine word foresaw history and writing according to the letter, so as to nourish the one born according to flesh to Abraham first with words according to flesh, and so that there might first be the one from the slave woman, in order that after this the one from the free woman and through the promise might be born. Why this was taken up can be understood: the foreskin of the heart comes before circumcision. So we need to take the word that cleanses the doctrines and removes everything that has come to be in us according to false opinion. This, then, is putting away the foreskin of our heart. For if the heart is, for us, what has the ruling principle—where the thoughts are, from which the reasonings go out—the one who removes evil reasonings removes 'the foreskin of the heart'; the one who puts away false opinion is circumcised as to the foreskin of his heart and becomes a man of Judah and one dwelling in Jerusalem, being circumcised.

But if someone does not put away the foreskin of his heart, let us see what the word threatens him: 'Lest my wrath go out,' it says, 'like fire and be kindled, and there will be none to quench it.' So the wrath of the Lord goes out like fire upon those not circumcised to God, upon those who have not put away the foreskin of their heart, 'and there will be none to quench it from before the wickedness of their practices.' That fire has as its matter the wickedness of our practices. Where there is no wickedness of practices, the fire has nowhere to spread.

That the matter of that fire is the wickedness of practices, hear the prophet saying: 'And there will be none to quench it from before the wickedness of your practices.' 'Announce in Judah, and let it be heard in Jerusalem; say, announce, signal with a trumpet upon the earth, and cry aloud.' These things announced, he says, say in Judah to those from the tribe of Judah of Christ—'for it is clear that our Savior has risen from Judah.'

title: Trumpet the word; flee into the walled city
english: 'Signal with a trumpet upon the earth.' The lofty word—the one that wakes the hearer, that prepares him for the fight against the passions and against the activities of opposing powers, that prepares him for the heavenly festivals (for it is said with a view to both)—is taken as a trumpet.

In Numbers such a word is a trumpet. For example, the word commands me—and anyone else to whom it is given who wills and has sought the mind of the Scriptures—to make 'silver trumpets, hammered work.' So the word says: 'Signal with a trumpet upon the earth, and cry aloud; say: Gather yourselves and let us enter the walled cities.' The word of God does not want us to enter an unwalled city, but into the church of the living God, walled by the strength of the Word—for he is the wall. In the seventeenth Psalm it also lies that God is a wall. 'Taking it up, flee into Zion.' As many of you as are outside Zion, 'taking it up, flee into Zion; hurry, do not stand still.' You who are in progress, hurry to the Lookout, 'for I am bringing evils from the north and a great crushing'—evils brought 'from the north'—from the opposing one, the north, as has often been said. Whoever is found not hurrying and not entering 'into the walled cities,' not becoming 'in the churches of God,' but standing outside, will himself be caught by the enemies and destroyed. Who is the enemy? Let us see from what follows how it is said: 'A lion has gone up from his den; destroying nations he has carried them off.' This is the enemy we must flee. A lion pursues us. Who is this? Peter teaches, saying: 'Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may swallow; resist him, firm in the faith.' And according to the ninth Psalm he 'lies in wait in secret; he lies in wait like a lion in his den.' And this lion does not lie in wait by day, but when night has come. For according to the hundred-and-third Psalm: 'You set darkness, and it became night. In it all the beasts of the wood will pass through, young lions roaring to snatch and to seek from God food for themselves.'

title: The lion from the den; put on sackcloth
english: 'A lion has gone up from his den.' Where? When? He is down, having fallen; he has come down into the lowest parts of the earth. 'A lion has gone up from his den.' You are a human being; you are higher than the devil. For you are stronger than he, whatever you may be. He, because of wickedness, is below. So 'a lion has gone up from his den; destroying nations he has carried them off.' Having gone up from his den—the place belonging to his own punishment—'destroying nations he has carried them off; he has gone out from his place to make your land a desolation.' He wants your land, about which we spoke a little earlier. He wants each of us to be pastured on.

So he comes 'to make your land' desolate, so that the lion may trample the seeds, so that he may make your land empty. 'And your cities will be torn down because they are not inhabited.' Upon these things, gird yourselves with sackcloth.

Since then a lion has gone up and a lion threatens you and wants to wipe out your land, gird sackcloth, weep and mourn, call on God through prayers, that he may destroy this lion from you and you may not fall into his mouth. For 'as when the shepherd snatches from a lion's mouth two legs or a lobe of an ear'—this lion seeks to take you by the ears, so that by your greediness, casting false words beside you, he may drive you from the truth; he wants to snatch your feet from the truth and devour them. But you gird sackcloth and beat your breast and weep and cry out, seeing the enemy who has come, so that 'the wrath of the Lord's anger' may turn away from you, and when the wrath has turned you may be able, in freedom from care—the lion no longer slipping in on you, because you have entered the walled city—to glorify the God who delivers you in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the power forever and ever.
Amen.

title: Eyes of the Lord and Virtues
english: Lord, your eyes are fixed on faith, as 'the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous,' for they turn from the unrighteous, so the eyes of the Lord are on faith, turning from unbelief. Therefore, the one who understands rightly says in prayer, 'Lord, your eyes are on faith.' What is written here is 'Lord, your eyes are on faith.' Since 'if a wise word is heard by a man of understanding, he will praise it and add to it,' see how much the Lord does, 'your eyes are on faith.' Paul says, 'Now faith, hope, love remain, but the greatest of these is love.' As the eyes of the Lord are on faith, so also on hope, so also on love.

Since the Spirit is power, purity, and self-control, the eyes of the Lord are on love, so the eyes of the Lord are on power, so the eyes of the Lord are on self-control... the eyes of the Lord on justice. Thus, the eyes of the Lord on all virtues. If you wish to have the rays of the Lord's intelligible eyes shine upon you, take up the virtues. And it will be as 'Lord, your eyes are on faith,' so 'Lord, your eyes' on each thing you acquire. And if you are so great, as the Lord's eyes shine upon you, you will say, 'The light of your face has been shown upon us, Lord.'

title: Divine Punishment and Spiritual Numbness
english: Then regarding the sinners, let us consider what is said: 'You have chastised them and they did not suffer. These are the sensible chastisements offered to bodies, whether the afflicted will or not, causing them pain; but the chastisements of God are such that some of the afflicted suffer, and some of the afflicted do not.'

Let us see if we can explain what it means to suffer from God's chastisements and what it means not to suffer, and that those who do not suffer from God's chastisements are evil, but those who suffer are blessed. For Wisdom says: 'Who will give me a chastisement upon my mind and a seal upon my lips of deceitful ones, that I may not be ashamed of my ignorance, and my sins may not destroy me?' Pay attention to 'Who will give me a chastisement upon my mind?' Does not this mean that the mind is chastised? The chastisements of the Lord chastise the mind; for a word that lays hold of the soul and brings it to a felt sense of what has been sinned, and so scourges it. But the chastisements chastise the blessed one suffering upon the chastisements, for the things said are fulfilled in him, and he does not despise the one rebuking him from himself.

title: Spiritual Hardness and the Hardened Heart
english: They have hardened their faces above the rock; understand this from the more physical. Those who hear reproving words about sin blush and sink down and fall beneath the word of their reprover. But those are such that they are unblushing, not ashamed of what they are reproved for, what they have sinned. Therefore, if you were to speak about those who do not blush, 'They have hardened their faces above the rock,' if you have understood this upon the physical, turn with me in the word to the soul's face, about which it is said, 'Then face to face.' And see a firm soul, such as the heart of Pharaoh, hardened so that it stands as a counterpart to what is spoken and as if rejecting what is said, not shaped according to what is spoken.

For there you will find that 'They have hardened their faces above the rock and did not wish to turn back.' And I said, 'Perhaps they are poor, because they did not wish to know the way of the Lord and the judgment of God.' I will go to the stout and speak to them. Understanding this about those who do not wish to be taught, who do not understand the stripes of God, he says having understood their cause. Their soul is poor. 'And I said, 'Perhaps they are poor, because they could not, because they did not know the way of the Lord and the judgment of God.' 'I will go to the stout and speak to them.' The stout are called in praise of the soul. And among the Hellenes the term 'stout' is constantly used for the greatness of the rational soul.

title: Divine Judgment and Mercy
english: The one judging the condemned grants place and does not immediately bear the end of punishment upon the transgressor. Therefore, 'judging briefly, he punishes.' This is exemplified in Leviticus, where prior punishments are recorded before subsequent penalties. The Lord says, 'If you do not turn back, I will add seven more plagues.' Another punishment is again described: 'If you do not turn back, but go astray, I will go with you in a sideways manner.' You will find God measuring punishments with mercy, as He desires to lead the transgressor to repentance, not wholly destroying them.

Thus, as much as occurred regarding the people through speech, the word threatens them and says they will be convinced after these things. 'In those days, the Lord your God will not strike you to destruction,' if these things especially reach even the future punishments, unless one who has power from things occurring in life regarding the people turns to them. For I would say, as 'they worship heavenly things by example and shadow,' so the people were punished by example and shadow of true punishments for their sins, as all punishment under the law and prophets contains the shadow of true punishments.

Therefore, since their end upon sins did not occur but at a final time, there will never be punishment upon the transgressors after the exodus. The end upon Jerusalem was when the captivity of Nebuchadnezzar occurred. Although someone might say that even then there was no end, nor upon the Maccabees. But the end of the people is upon the presence of my Lord Jesus Christ. For the Savior did not say to them, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' as He did not forgive them. When He wept over Jerusalem, saying, 'Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I desired to gather your children as a bird gathers its brood under its wings, and you would not!' 'Behold, your house is left to you desolate.' The house is left, surrounded by armies of Jerusalem, as the desolation of it has drawn near. Then after their transgression, salvation came to us. They were punished, but the end did not come upon them as the presence of my Lord Jesus.

title: Divine Punishments and Their Numbers
english: I consider that for us also such things may be, and some punishments may occur, so that these may not have a second punishment but be satisfied with the first, others may come even to the second, not indeed to the third, others may come even to the fourth. For the 'I will add seven plagues' signifies a mystery of one by one being inflicted, and the second, and the third, up to the seven mentioned for some. Not all are struck with seven plagues; rather, some I suppose will be struck with seven, others with five, others with four, others with three or two, and the most helpless among all in punishments I consider to be struck with one. Therefore, God knows the things regarding the plagues. Hence it is written here at the beginning of the reading: 'And it will be in those days... I will not make an end for you. Not an end in those days; for there are some days when He will make those He wills for an end.'

title: Idolatry and Divine Judgment
english: And it will be when you say, 'For what reason did the Lord God do all these evils to us?' And you will say to them, 'Because you abandoned me and served other gods in your land, so in a land not your own.'

The sons of Israel had the holy land, the temple, the house of prayer. They should have worshipped God. Transgressing the divine commands, they became idolaters and took in idols from Damascus, as written in the Books, and other idols from the land.

Will you cast out the food and drink? God is yours. Do you honor money as a great good and the wealth below? God is the Mammon and Lord. For Jesus said to the lovers of money: 'You cannot serve God and Mammon.'

If anyone in the church of God, while present, worships other gods, making unworthy things divine, they will be cast into a foreign land to worship the gods they once served. Let the greedy be expelled from the church, and the glutton be outside the church.
Now we are in a foreign land, and we pray to reverse this, as the sons of Israel did in the holy land.

They worshipped foreign gods in the holy land; we worship the foreign god of this land, foreign to earthly matters. The ruler of this age reigns here, and God is foreign to his children. I do not mean the creator of the world, but the God of evil, foreign to present sins.
Amen.

title: The Three Virtues Assigned to Earth, World, and Heaven
english: The prophet of God received the three virtues, as it were—strength, wisdom, and prudence—and assigned to each a fitting work: to strength he gave the earth, to wisdom the inhabited world, and to prudence the heavens.
For hear the word saying: 'The Lord who made the earth by his strength, who established the world by his wisdom, and by his prudence stretched out the heavens.'

And we too, concerning our earth (for it was spoken to Adam: 'We need the strength of God, and without God's power we are not able to accomplish these things, which are not according to the prudence of the flesh,' and 'the mortified members of the flesh...'), it will be according to the will of the Spirit, since 'the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit are put to death,' as the apostle says.
'Lord, therefore, the one who made the earth in his strength.'
